query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted thermo‐mechanical processing treatment—specifically, moderate cold rolling followed by a controlled low‐temperature annealing—will refine the lamellar microstructure of the as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and promote the formation of coherent, fine precipitates. This microstructural refinement will synergistically enhance yield and fracture strength, improve room‐temperature creep resistance, and mitigate localized corrosion, thereby better meeting the performance requirements for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations and long‐term mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Apply a thermo‐mechanical treatment consisting of an 8–10% thickness reduction via cold rolling immediately thereafter followed by short-time annealing at approximately 700°C to refine lamellar spacing and induce fine, coherent secondary precipitates.
generation.conditions: Performance tests conducted at room temperature and up to 700°C; exposure to simulated corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution or salt spray) and long-term mechanical loading conditions to assess creep behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined dual-phase lamellar structure with decreased interlamellar spacing and a dispersion of nano-scale, coherent precipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation motion and crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: Cold rolling introduces a high density of defects which, upon subsequent controlled annealing, triggers recovery and precipitation processes that refine the lamellar spacing and generate fine secondary phases. These microstructural features enhance dislocation pinning, delay creep deformation, and reduce the sites for corrosive attack by limiting high-energy interphase boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as‐cast state, the treated alloy will have a higher yield and fracture strength (with an expected improvement on the order of 10–20% or more pending optimization), improved ductility retention, more stable creep resistance at room temperature, and enhanced corrosion resistance under aggressive environmental conditions.
generation.baseline: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA in its as‐cast, uniform fine lamellar state that currently exhibits insufficient strength and ductility for industrial fastener applications.
generation.boundary: Operating temperatures up to 700°C; mechanical loading durations sufficient to reveal room-temperature creep behavior; corrosion tests conducted in environments mimicking industrial service conditions (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution or equivalent salt spray exposure) over standard test periods.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements and the optimal processing parameters (rolling reduction percentage, annealing temperature and duration) are not precisely known and require systematic experimental optimization. Additionally, potential trade-offs between increasing strength and preserving ductility need further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA fastener samples – a control group in the as-cast state and a test group subjected to the proposed cold rolling (8–10% thickness reduction) and annealing (700°C for a controlled short duration) treatment. Characterize the microstructure via SEM and TEM to confirm refined lamellar spacing and the formation of fine precipitates. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700°C), long-term room-temperature creep tests under a fixed load, and standardized corrosion tests (e.g., immersion in 3.5% NaCl solution or salt spray exposure).
measurements: Yield strength and fracture strength from tensile tests
Creep strain vs. time under constant load at room temperature
Corrosion metrics such as current density and corrosion potential
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 10% increase in yield strength and comparable or improved ductility, along with measurable enhancements in creep and corrosion resistance) compared to the as-cast control, or if any critical property falls below the industrial application thresholds, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: These results showed that the yield strength (1437 ± 26 MPa), tensile strength (1562 ± 33 MPa), and elongation (14 ± 1%) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after annealing at low temperature were significantly improved compared with the as-cast alloy. Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit an excellent balance of toughness and strength at room temperature. However, there is still an immediate requirement to design structural components with more strength and ductility due to the increasing technical requirements and harsher operating environments in industrial applications. The demand for stronger and more ductile structural elements has increased as airplane components have become more demanding and technical standards have advanced. Therefore, it is of significance to develop a new eutectic high-entropy alloy with superior properties based on AlCoCrFeNi2.1.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
